takeaway: OrchFS partitions arbitrary writes into aligned, parallel direct I/O for a high-bandwidth SSD and small residual NVM writes, optimizing the request-to-I/O transformation itself.
background: Applications issue byte-offset writes, but file systems convert them into page-aligned block I/O. Modern SSDs achieve peak bandwidth through internal parallelism and prefer larger page-aligned transfers; byte-addressable NVM instead handles small unaligned persistence efficiently but costs more per byte.
villain: Existing SSD file systems align writes through read-modify-write, copy and manage pages in the page cache, then often submit too little explicit concurrency. Even large direct writes can undersaturate a fast SSD, while hybrid systems typically absorb most traffic in NVM or merely separate small from large requests.
approach: OrchFS splits every write into 32-KB-aligned SSD blocks, 4-KB NVM pages, and residual NVM Upage chunks. A heterogeneous radix tree maps all units, while dedicated interlaced threads use direct SSD writes, buffered SSD reads, and memory-semantic NVM access in parallel; background migration consolidates NVM fragments to SSD.
impact: The design shows that a small NVM complement can unlock rather than replace SSD bandwidth. It reframes I/O transformation—alignment, path selection, splitting, and concurrency—as a first-class file-system policy.

evaluation.overview: Microbenchmarks cover diverse sizes, reads/writes, components, NVM space, concurrency, and SSD generations; Filebench, synchronous LevelDB/YCSB, GridGraph, and aging experiments evaluate mixed and real workloads.
evaluation.implemented: A from-scratch LibFS/KernelFS prototype exposing more than 30 POSIX APIs, with a three-unit data layout, O(1) write partitioner, heterogeneous radix tree, default 4 NVM and 32 SSD I/O threads, logical metadata journaling, leases, and NVM-to-SSD migration.
evaluation.setting: Dual 28-core Xeon Gold 6348 processors, 256 GB DRAM, 128-GB Optane PM, and a 3.84-TB PCIe 4 Samsung PM9A3 SSD; selected tests use a PCIe 5 PM1743 or two PCIe 4 SSDs. Results average at least three runs.

results.text: Across single-thread random-write sizes, OrchFS reduces latency by up to 29.76× versus SSD file systems, 3.49× versus NVM file systems, and 7.16× versus hybrid NVM/SSD file systems.
For 1-MB random writes, only about 4.7% of file data resides in NVM, yet OrchFS cuts write latency by 68.4% and 72.4% versus ext4 and F2FS.
OrchFS reaches 1.76×–15.12× baseline Filebench throughput with 16 threads and runs 20-iteration GridGraph workloads 1.69×–3.20× faster across three graphs.

limitations: OrchFS needs auxiliary byte-addressable NVM and uses discontinued Optane in evaluation. All-small-write workloads reside in NVM until migration and can degenerate into a hierarchy. The prototype implements a subset of POSIX, guarantees atomic metadata but not atomic data by default, and some baselines provide stricter write atomicity. Fixed granularity and thread counts require retuning for other devices.
phd_group_signal: The work derives a design from careful latency decomposition rather than accepting the legacy storage path. It spans device behavior, file layout, indexing, concurrency, userspace/kernel architecture, consistency, and aging—useful territory for storage-systems research.

claims.text: OrchFS transforms aligned middles of writes into SSD-block I/O and maps unaligned heads, tails, and overwrites into NVM pages or chunk-bearing Upages without host or SSD read-modify-write.
Dedicated threads interlace 32-KB address ranges so SSD writes are aligned, direct, and parallel, while SSD reads retain page caching and NVM I/O follows a memory-semantic path.
